title: Data is everything
blurb: AI learns from data — explore a real dataset and discover how patterns (and bias) are born.

steps.title: Where does AI get its smarts?
steps.body:
Last time you learned AI learns from **examples**. A big pile of examples has a name: **data**.

Data is the food an AI eats. Feed it good data and it gets smart. Feed it bad data and it gets… not so smart. Let's see what data actually looks like.

steps.title: What data looks like
steps.body:
Data is usually just a **table** — like a spreadsheet.

Each **row** is one example (one flower, one photo, one song). Each **column** is one thing we measured about it. That's it. No magic — just a tidy list of examples.

steps.title: Features and labels
steps.body:
Two words pros use constantly:

- **Features** = the things we *measure* (a flower's petal length, its height…).
- **Label** = the *answer* we want (what kind of flower it is).

The AI's job: look at the **features** and guess the **label**.

steps.title: Feature or label?
steps.question: We want an AI to guess a flower's *kind* from its *petal length*. Which one is the label?
steps.explain: The **kind of flower** is the label — it's the answer we want. Petal length is a feature we measure to guess it.

steps.title: Let's explore real data
steps.body:
Below is a tiny dataset of **30 flowers** — daisies, tulips, and roses — each with a few measurements.

Put different measurements on the **X** and **Y** axes and watch what happens. Can you find axes where the three kinds split into clear groups?

steps.title: Explore the flowers
steps.body: Change the X and Y axes. Each dot is one flower, colored by its kind.

steps.title: That's a pattern!
steps.body:
See how the colors form **clusters**? Daisies bunch in one corner, roses in another. The AI doesn't need anyone to *tell* it the rule — it can *see* that big petals usually mean "rose."

**Finding clusters like these is exactly what a classifier does.**

steps.title: Reading the chart
steps.question: When the kinds form separate clusters on the chart, what does that mean for the AI?
choices: The features are useful — they help tell the kinds apart
steps.explain: Clear clusters = useful features. If everything overlapped in one blob, the AI would have a much harder time.

steps.title: Better features, smarter AI
steps.body:
Some measurements separate the flowers well; others barely help. Picking **good features** is half the battle in real AI.

It's like guessing someone's favorite sport: their *height* might help a little, but "do they own a soccer ball?" helps a lot more. Good features carry the answer.

steps.title: Garbage in, garbage out
steps.body:
Here's the rule that explains most AI failures: **an AI can only be as good as its data.**

Messy, wrong, or missing data → a confused AI. Clean, clear data → a sharp one. The data matters more than the computer.

steps.title: The sneaky problem: balance
steps.body:
Now imagine our flower data had **28 roses** and only **2 daisies**.

The AI would barely know what a daisy looks like — so it'd guess "rose" almost every time. Not because roses are special, but because that's mostly what it *saw*. This lopsidedness has a name: **bias**.

steps.title: Spot the bias
steps.question: An AI that sorts fruit was trained on 100 apples and 4 bananas. What will probably happen?
choices: It leans toward guessing 'apple' because that's mostly what it saw
steps.explain: Exactly — a lopsided dataset makes a lopsided AI. Balanced examples are the fix.

steps.title: Where bias really comes from
steps.body:
Bias isn't the computer being mean. It comes from the **data we collect**.

If the examples we gather miss certain groups, the AI misses them too. That's why real AI teams work so hard to gather **fair, balanced** data — it's one of the most important jobs in the whole field.

steps.title: Why this matters in real life
steps.body:
This isn't just about flowers. The same idea decides whether AI is **fair**:

- A face system that only learned from a few kinds of faces works worse for everyone else.
- A voice assistant trained on one accent struggles with others.

Good, balanced data is how we build AI that works for **everybody**.

steps.title: Recap
steps.question: What's the best way to keep an AI from becoming biased?
choices: Collect balanced, fair examples of every group
steps.explain: Balanced, fair data is the answer. The AI learns whatever the data teaches it — so we make sure the data is fair.

steps.title: What you learned 🎉
steps.body:
- **Data** = a table of examples (rows) with **features** (columns) and a **label** (the answer)
- Good **features** make the kinds form clear **clusters**
- **Garbage in, garbage out** — data quality beats computer speed
- **Bias** is born from lopsided data; **balanced, fair data** is the cure

**Next up:** instead of sorting things into kinds, you'll teach an AI to **predict a number** — that's called *regression*.
